Baseball. A bat-and-ball sport played between two teams of nine players, typically across nine innings on a diamond-shaped field with four bases.

Emerging in nineteenth-century America as a refinement of earlier bat-and-ball games, baseball became enshrined as the nation's pastime and claims a central place in American culture, history, and identity. The sport's blend of individual achievement, strategic team play, and statistical depth has generated the world's most voluminous sports literature and analysis.

Baseball is played on a diamond with four bases—home, first, second, and third. The batting team scores a run by hitting the ball and circling all bases, while the fielding team records outs through strikeouts, force plays, or tag plays. Each batter faces a pitcher throwing from a mound and accumulates three strikes to be struck out or draws walks from four balls, making plate discipline and pitch selection central to the game.

The sport's statistical sophistication has made it an intellectual pursuit. Earned run average, batting average, wins above replacement, and sabermetrics enable deeper analysis than nearly any other sport. Professional baseball in the United States has been organized under the Major League Baseball structure since the late nineteenth century, with the American League and National League competing for prestige.

The World Series championship, first played in 1903, is the oldest championship series in North American professional sports and remains baseball's supreme competition. Iconic franchises like the New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox, and Los Angeles Dodgers have accumulated deep histories spanning generations, creating powerful traditions and passionate regional identities. Evolution from earlier bat-and-ball games like rounders and cricket into its modern form occurred across the nineteenth century, with the Knickerbocker Club codifying standardized rules in 1845 that became foundational to modern play.
